# Lab 6 — System Optimization

**Scenario:** `fp-06-system-optimization` · runs of ~18 minutes each

::: {.callout-tip}
## Hands you'll need
Everything from Labs 3–5; if it's been a while, the Practice Range's six
drills are a five-minute refresher.
:::

Every previous lab isolated one idea and handed you one dial. The capstone
takes the dials away. The factory is squeezed from both ends at once — a
supplier who won't slow down and a customer who won't wait — and the
toolbox contains every remedy this course has taught: faster machines,
buffer chests, circuit components. Most combinations of them fail. The lab
is over when you can say *why* the ones that fail, fail — before running
them.

## The system

The familiar fast → slow → fast line (37.5 / 30 / 45 workpieces per
minute), with two new external facts:

- **A scheduled supplier.** 36 workpieces/min arrive on a fixed schedule,
  whether you're ready or not, into a warehouse holding at most 100 with a
  10-unit overflow yard behind it. **Deliveries that find both full are
  lost forever** — the supply-loss metric counts them against everything
  the supplier scheduled. The warehouse starts nearly full (90) so the
  line never starves at startup — but do not mistake the quiet opening
  minutes for health. An empty line swallows a lot of material while its
  belts and machine buffers fill, and that cold-start gulp drains the
  warehouse; the structural 6/min surplus then spends the first stretch
  of the run silently refilling it. The loss doesn't start until the
  buffers are full again — and then it never stops.
- **A customer**, as in Lab 5: 33/min demanded, 30 s patience, FIFO
  backlog, on-time item rate watching.

Arithmetic the learner can do at the whiteboard before touching anything:
the line's constraint produces 30/min. The supplier delivers 36. The
customer wants 33. Every minute, 6 units pile up at the gate and 3 units
of demand go unserved. *Both* ends bleed, from *one* cause.

## The objectives — and why there is no score

```text
Requirements:  on-time item rate >= 95%   AND   supply loss <= 2%
Preference:    minimize average WIP
```

The requirements are a conjunction: pass both or the run is infeasible.
The preference only ranks runs *within* the feasible set — `fisl compare`
prints an infeasible run's WIP but marks it as not competing. There is no
weighted score, deliberately: a score would let 7.33 units of WIP buy back
a failed customer, and Lab 5 already showed where that leads. An
incomplete measurement evaluates as UNDETERMINED — never quietly as a
pass or a failure.

## Run 1 — watch it fail twice

Run the baseline untouched and watch both requirements fail on one
screen: the on-time rate sinking as backlog accumulates (it ends the
window at **33.3%** against the 95% requirement), and — later than you'd
expect — the supply-loss row waking up, finishing at **6.1%** against
the 2% cap. Note *when* each failure becomes visible. The service
failure shows within minutes; the supply failure hides for roughly ten
minutes behind refilling buffers, then arrives all at once and
permanently — the measured 6.1% is ~33 units lost at ~6/min over the
window's last stretch, exactly the warehouse arithmetic. A ten-minute
audit of this factory would have reported one problem; the system has
two. One more honest cell: the baseline's p95 customer wait prints
**censored** — enough demand was simply never served that the tail wait
has no measurable value. Walk the line mid-run and collect the full
diagnosis kit from earlier labs: which machine never rests (Lab 2,
throughput pinned at 30/min), who is blocked and who is starved (Lab 4:
5.5% blocked above the constraint, 11.3% starved below), where the queue
sits (Lab 3, average WIP 57), what the customer sees (Lab 5).

## Run 2 — spend your effort

Two committed reference runs bracket the space; your own combinations are
the real assignment.

- **A — buffer the inflow** (the seductive partial fix): splice a chest
  into the belt upstream of the constraint. Supply loss stops — measured
  **0.0%**, intake jumps to 37.47/min — and the service failure *doesn't
  move*: 33.1% on time, indistinguishable from the baseline's 33.3%,
  while average WIP nearly doubles to 102.4 (167 at the bell). One
  requirement green, one red: **INFEASIBLE**. You moved the loss from
  the supplier's scrap heap into your own inventory account, at full
  carrying cost.
- **B — relieve the constraint**: swap the middle machine for the 45/min
  model. The line's pace moves to 37.5/min — above the supplier's 36
  *and* the customer's 33 — and **both requirements pass with one
  action**, because both symptoms shared one cause: 100% on time, p95
  wait 1.47 s, zero loss, throughput 37.53/min. Average WIP settles at
  **33.57** — lower than the untouched baseline's, and the preference
  value the feasible set is ranked by.

The measured reference table:

| run | TH | avg WIP | on-time | p95 wait | supply loss | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| baseline | 30.00/min | 57.04 | 33.3% | censored | 6.1% | INFEASIBLE (both) |
| A — buffer | 30.00/min | 102.41 | 33.1% | censored | 0.0% | INFEASIBLE (service) |
| B — upgrade | 37.53/min | **33.57** | 100.0% | 1.47 s | 0.0% | **feasible** |

```sh
fisl solutions scenarios/factory-physics/fp06-system-optimization --run \
    --json course/data/lab-06-comparison.json
```

Then go beyond the references: add B's upgrade *and* Lab 3's pull gate —
how low can average WIP go while both requirements hold? That number, and
your explanation of what limits it, is the capstone deliverable.

## Debrief

- Solution A passed the requirement everyone upstream could see and failed
  the one the customer feels. Which dashboards in a real company report
  the first kind of number? Who reports the second?
- The baseline's supply loss was invisible for most of the run — buffer
  space absorbed a structural 6/min deficit until it didn't. How long
  would a measurement window have to be before you'd trust a "no loss"
  reading? What plays the role of that buffer space in a real supply
  agreement?
- Why did one machine swap fix two apparently unrelated problems? State
  the general rule about symptoms and constraints.
- Now raise the supplier to 40/min (above M1's 37.5 ceiling). No machine
  swap fixes intake. What are your options, and what does each cost in
  which currency — loss, inventory, or capacity? (This is the first
  scenario in the course with no clean answer. That's the point.)
- Across seven labs you measured stocks, flows, constraints, states,
  service, and loss — always with declared boundaries, windows, and
  denominators. Which of those habits survives contact with a real
  operation where nobody hands you a conservation ledger?

## What the whole course assumed away

Determinism, to the end. Every rate in this factory is a constant, so
every diagnosis is an arithmetic identity and every fix either works or
doesn't. Real systems add variability — and with it, buffers earn keep,
utilization near 100% becomes dangerous rather than merely pointless, and
"how much capacity is enough" becomes a distribution question. The
variability course starts exactly where this lab's 40/min homework leaves
off: when the clean answer stops existing, what do you buy insurance
with — inventory, capacity, or time?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Instructor notes

- All numbers in this chapter are measured (reference dataset in
  `course/data/lab-06-comparison.json`): baseline INFEASIBLE on both
  requirements (33.3% on time, 6.1% loss, TH 30.00/min, WIP 57.04, p95
  censored); `a-buffer-the-inflow` INFEASIBLE on service alone (33.1% on
  time, 0.0% loss, WIP 102.41 and climbing — final 167);
  `b-upgrade-constraint` feasible (100% on time, p95 1.47 s, 0.0% loss,
  TH 37.53/min, WIP 33.57 — the preference value).
- Baseline mechanics (learned the hard way — a 10-minute window measured
  only 0.8% loss): the cold-start belt fill plus machine buffers drain
  the warehouse during warmup, so the measured window opens with tens of
  units of free warehouse space. The 6/min structural surplus spends
  ~12 minutes (from supply start) refilling that space before overflow
  begins; thereafter essentially the full 6/min is lost. The measured
  6.1% over 15 minutes is ~33 of 540 scheduled units — the last ~5½
  minutes of the window losing at the full deficit rate, exactly the
  whiteboard arithmetic.
- The masking effect is part of the lesson (see Run 1 and the debrief):
  transient buffer space hides a structural deficit; short audits report
  health. The baseline's censored p95 is a second teachable: with enough
  never-served demand, the tail wait honestly has no value.
- The in-game panel shows all three objective *rules* from READY onward
  (visibility discloses them); verdicts appear only in the post-run
  report — no provisional in-game pass/fail.
- The supply-loss denominator is the supplier's *scheduled* quantity in
  the window (telemetry records both scheduled arrivals and overflow
  losses); the metric is a fraction with exact integers behind it.
:::
